title: Gases and the Absolute Temperature Scale

content.text: Gases and the Absolute Temperature Scale

Gases are all around us, yet they are invisible and often overlooked. The air you breathe, the carbon dioxide in fizzy drinks, and the helium in balloons are all gases, and they all follow remarkably simple and predictable rules. In this lesson, we will explore the behaviour of gases using the particle model, understand why scientists use the Kelvin temperature scale, and learn the mathematical laws that describe how gas pressure, volume, and temperature are related to each other.
These gas laws are not just theoretical curiosities. They are used every day in engineering, medicine, scuba diving, weather forecasting, and countless other applications.

The Celsius scale is convenient for everyday use, but it has an important limitation for physics: 0°C is not truly zero. At 0°C, water freezes, but the particles still have kinetic energy and are still moving. We need a temperature scale where zero really means zero, where the particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy.
This is the Kelvin scale, and its zero point is called
is the temperature at which particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy. No further energy can be removed. This occurs at
The size of one kelvin is exactly the same as the size of one degree Celsius. The scales are simply offset by 273.
Note: We write "K" for kelvin, not "°K". There is no degree symbol with kelvin.

The Kelvin scale is essential when working with gas laws because gas behaviour is directly related to the absolute temperature. If you use Celsius in gas law calculations, you will get incorrect answers. This is because the gas laws depend on ratios of temperatures, and ratios only work correctly when the scale starts at true zero.

does not double the kinetic energy of the gas particles. But doubling the Kelvin temperature from

Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of their container. Each collision exerts a tiny force on the wall. The total force from billions of collisions per second, divided by the area of the wall, gives the gas pressure.
: More particles means more collisions, so higher pressure.
: Faster particles hit the walls harder and more frequently, so higher pressure.
: A smaller container means particles hit the walls more frequently, so higher pressure.
Since the speed of gas particles depends on temperature, gas pressure is directly related to temperature (when volume is constant).

Boyle's law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure is inversely proportional to the volume.

If the volume of a container is reduced (compressed), the particles have less space to move around in. They hit the walls more frequently, so the pressure increases. If the volume is doubled, the particles have twice as much space, hit the walls half as frequently, and the pressure halves.

Charles's law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, the volume is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

When the temperature of a gas increases, the particles move faster and collide with the walls of the container more forcefully. If the container can expand (for example, a balloon), the gas pushes the walls outward until the pressure inside equals the pressure outside. The volume increases in direct proportion to the absolute temperature.

The pressure law states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

When the temperature increases, particles move faster. In a fixed-volume container, they cannot push the walls outward, so they hit the walls harder and more often. This increases the pressure in direct proportion to the absolute temperature.

The three individual gas laws can be combined into a single equation that relates pressure, volume, and temperature:
This is useful when all three quantities change simultaneously. Each of the individual laws can be derived from this equation by holding one variable constant.
Note: In all gas law calculations, temperature must always be in kelvin.

| Law | Constant | Relationship | Equation |
|-----|----------|-------------|----------|
| Boyle's law | Temperature | $P \propto 1/V$ | $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ |
| Charles's law | Pressure | $V \propto T$ | $V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2$ |
| Pressure law | Volume | $P \propto T$ | $P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2$ |
| Combined* | None | $PV/T = \text{const}$ | $P_1V_1/T_1 = P_2V_2/T_2$ |
Extension: The combined gas law goes beyond the IGCSE 0625 syllabus.*

The volume of the tyre remains approximately constant (tyres are rigid). When the temperature increases, the air molecules inside the tyre gain kinetic energy and move faster. They collide with the walls of the tyre more forcefully and more frequently. Since the tyre volume does not change significantly, the pressure increases.
Misconception 1: "You can use Celsius in gas law equations"

You must always use kelvin for temperature in gas law equations. Using Celsius will give incorrect results because the gas laws are based on proportional relationships that only hold true when temperature is measured from absolute zero.

is not doubling the absolute temperature. In kelvin, this is going from
Misconception 4: "Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with each other"

Gas pressure on a surface is caused by particles colliding with that surface. Collisions between gas particles themselves do not directly contribute to the pressure on the container walls, although they do affect the distribution of particle speeds.
Misconception 5: "All gas particles move at the same speed"

At any given temperature, gas particles have a range of speeds. Some move slowly, some move very fast, and most have speeds somewhere in the middle. The temperature determines the average kinetic energy, not the speed of every individual particle.
Misconception 6: "The gas laws only apply to ideal gases"

While the gas laws are perfectly accurate only for ideal gases, they work very well for real gases under normal conditions (moderate temperatures and pressures). Real gases only deviate significantly from ideal behaviour at very high pressures or very low temperatures.
